Rules / Cleanup

SK0234 The cast or type argument is redundant

A cast whose operand already has the cast's type, explicit method type arguments inference reproduces exactly, an array size that repeats the element count, and tuple component names the declared type already carries.

CategoryCleanup
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0
ReSharperRedundantCast (resharper_redundant_cast_highlighting)

Why

Each one is a conversion that converts nothing, and each is read as if it might. A cast makes a reader ask what the operand was before it; explicit type arguments make them ask what inference would have chosen; an array size makes them count the elements to see whether the two agree.

Example

Instead of:

var name = (string)text;
var items = Enumerable.Empty<int>().ToList<int>();
var row = new string[2] { "a", "b" };
(string Name, int Age) person = (Name: name, Age: 30);

Write:

var name = text;
var items = Enumerable.Empty<int>().ToList();
var row = new string[] { "a", "b" };
(string Name, int Age) person = (name, 30);

When it does not fire

⚠ A cast is not redundant merely because the types allow removing it, and this rule is written around that sentence. var x = (long)1; types x as long and var x = 1; types it as int. M((object)s) and M(s) call different overloads. flag ? (long)a : b infers a different type once the cast is gone. Roslyn's own IDE0004 is the standing example of getting this wrong, so Skala covers the one subset where none of those questions can be asked: an identity conversion, where the operand's type and the cast's type are the same symbol, confirmed by ClassifyConversion(...).IsIdentity. ⚠ This sentence used to name `SymbolEqualityComparer.IncludeNullability` as the comparison and that was never the code: GetTypeInfo on a TypeSyntax returns NullableAnnotation.None for every written type, string and string? alike, so that comparer rejects every cast including the identity ones — the first draft reported nothing at all, on any fixture. The comparison is SymbolEqualityComparer.Default, and nullability is asked separately: the written annotation from the syntax (cast.Type is NullableTypeSyntax) and the two flow states from the model. The expression's type is then unchanged by the deletion, so nothing downstream of it can change either. ⚠ Every widening, narrowing and boxing cast is therefore deliberately uncovered, including the upcast that is most of what RedundantCast reports in practice. That is a smaller rule on purpose; the negative fixture set records each declined shape. ⚠ Nullability is not a detail here: (string)maybeNull is typed string where its operand is string?, so the cast is what tells the flow analysis what the author knows, and a var declared from it would change type without it. ⚠ Tuples are excluded from the cast branch entirely and handled by the component-name branch, because ((int a, int b))(1, 2) and ((int, int))(1, 2) differ in the names the result carries. ⚠ Explicit method type arguments are removed only where re-binding the call without them reaches the identical constructed method — the same definition with different inferred type arguments does not count. ⚠ An array size is matched for one dimension only: a jagged or rectangular creation has sizes whose relationship to the initializer is not the flat count this compares against. ⚠ Tuple component names are dropped only under a written tuple type. Under var the names come from the literal and deleting them deletes them from the variable's type, and no semantic query separates those two cases because the resulting type is identical. ⚠ An invocation under a conditional access is refused, and the reason is a crash. values?.Where(…).Cast<string>() binds .Where(…) as a member binding whose receiver is the conditional access above it. The type-argument branch rewrites the node and binds the rewrite speculatively, which detaches it from that access, and Roslyn's own FindConditionalAccessNodeForBinding then dereferences null and throws a NullReferenceException out of the analyzer. It reached a report as nothing at all — an analyzer exception is AD0001 (#279), which skala check renames to SK9030 and does not fail a gate on (#295) — and it was found by asserting on AD0001 in the fixture harness rather than by reading the code. ⚠ Four of the family's eight inspections are not covered: RedundantExplicitArrayCreation (new object[] { "a", "b" } infers string[] once the type is dropped), RedundantExplicitNullableCreation, RedundantTypeArgumentsInsideNameof and PreferExplicitlyProvidedTupleComponentName, which asks for the opposite of what this rule does.
